\ednentry{
  id = {EDN-79},
  title = {The seller-grouped hash split stays, and its figures are reported with their spread over other splits},
  date = {2026-10-12},
  milestone = {M3: Quality Assurance},
  topic = {Evaluation Protocol, Data Splitting},
  participants = {@lukas2510, decided by the repository owner},
  decision = {The split stays as it is: whole sellers assigned by a hash of the seed and the seller key, 60/10/10/20, unstratified, with the committed seed.
What changes is the reporting: the model card states the distribution of every set, and a figure of the committed split is given with its spread over 20 other splits.
An adversarial-validation check is recorded once and not made a standing check, and the missing temporal split is a stated limitation.},
  rationale = {\emph{Alternatives considered:}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, topsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Option A (chosen): keep the grouped hash split and report the set distributions.}
\newline Pros: no rerun and no number moves a week before the delivery; adding sellers moves no seller already there, measured at 0.00\,\% of the rows when the \texttt{ES} listings join the pool, which is what FR-15's retrain comparison rests on; the committed draw is better balanced than 72\,\% of 1,000 seeds.
\newline Cons: the balance is the luck of this draw, not a property of the design, and Mercedes-Benz stays at 8.67\,\% of the calibration set against 13.54\,\% of the pool.
\item \textbf{Option B: a stratified-group split on \texttt{make}.}
\newline Pros: the largest gap of any make's share in any set to its pool share falls from 4.86 pp to 2.04 pp, and calibration reaches 11.5\,\% Mercedes-Benz.
\newline Cons: the assignment depends on all sellers at once, so 52.6\,\% of the existing rows change set when the \texttt{ES} listings join, about as many as a new seed moves, which confounds FR-15's before-and-after comparison; a full pipeline rerun and new split code, with every reported number changing; and it cannot balance the make either, because one dealer holds 25.2\,\% of the Mercedes-Benz listings and has to go somewhere whole.
\item \textbf{Option C (chosen, with A): repeated grouped splits, reporting the spread beside the single figure.}
\newline Pros: it answers what was never measured, how much a figure depends on which sellers landed where, in about 15 minutes and without touching the pipeline.
\newline Cons: an analysis script rather than a stage, so it has to be re-run by hand when the candidate or the data changes.
\item \textbf{Option D (recorded once): adversarial validation.}
\newline Pros: one classifier, AUC 0.495 on held-out sellers, so train and test are indistinguishable.
\newline Cons: nearly a tautology for a random assignment of sellers; run row-wise it reports 0.599, which is the dealer signature EDN-14 found and not a difference between the sets, so as a standing check it would mostly raise false alarms.
\item \textbf{Option E: choose a seed for a better mix.}
\newline Pros: none that survives a question.
\newline Cons: a new split selected by its outcome; and the committed seed already gives the most favourable SC-04 figure of 21 draws, so a reseed would either worsen that number or look chosen for it.
\item \textbf{Option F: a temporal split.}
\newline Pros: the strongest test for a price model.
\newline Cons: impossible, the snapshot has no listing dates; it is stated as a limitation.
\end{itemize}
\par
\emph{Why:} The question was whether the default split deserved to stay, and three measurements could have said no; none did.
The imbalance that prompted the issue has one cause, and it is not what the issue assumed: the largest seller group is a single dealer with 3,383 listings, 3,382 of them Mercedes-Benz, that landed in train, so train is raised (14.95\,\%, 9.97\,\% without it) rather than calibration being short, and the calibration share is at the 21st percentile of its own distribution over 1,000 seeds.
The verdict on the pooled criteria does not depend on the draw: over 20 other splits the candidate's test MdAPE is 6.73\,\% on average with a standard deviation of 0.27 pp, against 6.81\,\% committed, and SC-01 and SC-02 hold on all 20.
And SC-04's miss is not an artefact of it: cars older than 20 years are over the bound on 20 of 20 splits, at 18.3\,\% on average, so the committed 16.77\,\% understates the miss.
Against that, option B buys 2.8 pp of make balance for the one property the split was built for.
The same run puts EDN-73 in context: the validation MdAPE moves by 0.42 pp (standard deviation) between splits, more than the 0.16 pp the whole tuning grid spans on one.
The 20 splits share one pool of listings, so the spread describes how a figure moves with the assignment and is not a confidence interval for new data.
The issue's criterion that the UC2 interval coverage be checked per make is deferred to the work that builds the intervals: no model has an interval method and SC-05 is not measured, so there is nothing to compute a coverage from.},
  ai = {Information seeking, Alternative generation, Alternative assessment, Recommendation, Solution generation},
  response = {Accepted},
  assessment = {AI wrote and ran the evidence script against the stages' own split, feature and fit code, checked first that it reproduces the committed \texttt{metrics.\allowbreak{}json} exactly, and ran 20 seeds instead of the ten asked for after timing one.

It laid out the six options with their measured costs, recommended A with C, and stopped for the decision; Lukas chose A with C as recommended, with D recorded once and F as a limitation.
It also reported that the interval-coverage criterion could not be met and proposed deferring it rather than producing a number.
The recommendation was accepted without change because every claim in it is a line of the results file that can be re-run.},
